\chapter{Water, Tea, Milk, and Bread}
\label{ch:gu-request-food-drink}
\hlchaptermodality{14}

\begin{chapteropening}
\textbf{By the end of this chapter:} \emph{I can politely ask for water, tea, milk, or bread in Gujarati, name which of the four is a loanword and which have no settled root beyond Sanskrit, and explain why a word ending in -ī is not automatically feminine.}

The chapter closes on \gu{રોટલી}, the request that breaks the drink pattern: the reader produces all four requests with \gu{મહેરબાની} \gu{કરીને}, sorts \gu{પાણી} and \gu{દૂધ} (inherited, known root) against \gu{ચા} (loaned from Chinese by the overland route) against \gu{રોટલી} (inherited, root unknown), and uses \gu{પાણી}'s neuter gender despite its -ī ending to show that \gu{રોટલી}'s own feminine -ī is a hint, not a rule.
\end{chapteropening}

\section[pāṇī]{\gu{પાણી} — the first thing you'll actually ask for}

\label{lesson:GU-C10-paani}



\begin{quote}
\emph{Gamvũ} let you say what you like; \emph{madad karvī} let you ask for help. This chapter asks for something smaller and more frequent: a drink.
\end{quote}

\subsection*{You'll want to know first — one word}
\begin{quote}
\textbf{\gu{પાણી}} — \emph{pāṇī} — \textbf{water}
\end{quote}

\subsection*{The letters in this word}
\textbf{\gu{પ}} \emph{pa}, \textbf{\gu{ા}} the long-\emph{ā} sign, \textbf{\gu{ણ}} the retroflex \emph{ṇ} you already curled back in \emph{jāṇvũ}, then \textbf{\gu{ી}} long-\emph{ī}. No bar runs across the top of any of them — the headless tell, working the same way in a noun as it did in a verb.

\begin{grammarlens}[title={Grammar Lens: asking politely}]
\begin{quote}
\textbf{\gu{પાણી}, \gu{મહેરબાની} \gu{કરીને}.} — \emph{pāṇī, meherbānī karīne.} — \textbf{Water, please.}
\end{quote}

\textbf{\gu{મહેરબાની} \gu{કરીને}} \emph{meherbānī karīne} is built from \textbf{\gu{મહેરબાની}}, \textquotedblleft{}kindness\textquotedblright{} or \textquotedblleft{}favor,\textquotedblright{} plus \textbf{\gu{કરીને}}, \textquotedblleft{}having done\textquotedblright{} — the same \textbf{\gu{કરીને}/\gu{કરવી}} family you met in \textbf{\gu{મદદ} \gu{કરવી}}, \textquotedblleft{}to do a favor of help.\textquotedblright{} Literally: \textquotedblleft{}having done a kindness.\textquotedblright{} Name the item, add this, and you have a complete polite request with no verb for \textquotedblleft{}give\textquotedblright{} needed at all — the pattern this whole chapter will reuse.
\end{grammarlens}

\begin{cousinweb}
\textbf{pāṇī} comes from Sanskrit \textbf{pānīya}, \textquotedblleft{}that which is to be drunk,\textquotedblright{} built on \textbf{pā-}, \textquotedblleft{}to drink.\textquotedblright{} That root is Indo-European, *\emph{peh\textsubscript{3}(i)-}, and English holds two disguised pieces of it: \textbf{potion} and \textbf{poison} both come through Latin \emph{potare}, \textquotedblleft{}to drink\textquotedblright{} — a poison, etymologically, is just a drink gone wrong. Greek turned the same idea into \emph{sympotēs}, \textquotedblleft{}one who drinks together,\textquotedblright{} which English keeps as \textbf{symposium}. \emph{Pāṇī} is not a stranger to those words; it is what \textquotedblleft{}to drink\textquotedblright{} looks like when it never left the family that gave you \emph{jāṇvũ}'s Sanskrit cousin \emph{jñā-}.
\end{cousinweb}

\subsection*{Your turn}
\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item \emph{Say it:} \textbf{pāṇī} — water
  \item \emph{Say it:} \textbf{pāṇī, meherbānī karīne.} — water, please
  \item \emph{Match:} \textbf{karīne} against \textbf{madad karvī}'s own \textbf{kar-} root
  \item \emph{Trace it:} \emph{pā-} \textquotedblleft{}to drink\textquotedblright{} $\to$ \textbf{pāṇī}, and $\to$ \textbf{potion}, \textbf{poison}, \textbf{symposium}
  \item \emph{Run through:} \textbf{mane gujarātī game chhe}, then \textbf{pāṇī, meherbānī karīne} — liking and requesting, side by side
\end{itemize}

\begin{tcolorbox}[breakable,colback=teal!4,colframe=teal!35!black,title={Before you move on}]
Ask for water politely. (\emph{Pāṇī, meherbānī karīne.}) What does \emph{meherbānī karīne} mean word for word? (\textquotedblleft{}Having done a kindness.\textquotedblright{}) Which two English words for a drink, and one for a whole gathering of them, share \emph{pāṇī}'s root? (\textbf{Potion}, \textbf{poison}, \textbf{symposium}.)

Sources: \href{https://en.wiktionary.org/wiki/\%E0\%AA\%AA\%E0\%AA\%BE\%E0\%AA\%A3\%E0\%AB\%80}{Wiktionary: \gu{પાણી}}; \href{https://en.wiktionary.org/wiki/\%E0\%AA\%AE\%E0\%AA\%B9\%E0\%AB\%87\%E0\%AA\%B0\%E0\%AA\%AC\%E0\%AA\%BE\%E0\%AA\%A8\%E0\%AB\%80}{Wiktionary: \gu{મહેરબાની}}.
\end{tcolorbox}
\section[chā]{\gu{ચા} — the tea that went overland}

\label{lesson:GU-C10-chaa}



\begin{quote}
\emph{Pāṇī, meherbānī karīne} — water, please. The next drink uses the exact same pattern, and its own name has traveled further than water's ever needed to.
\end{quote}

\subsection*{You'll want to know first — one word}
\begin{quote}
\textbf{\gu{ચા}} — \emph{chā} — \textbf{tea}
\end{quote}

\begin{quote}
\textbf{\gu{ચા}, \gu{મહેરબાની} \gu{કરીને}.} — \emph{chā, meherbānī karīne.} — \textbf{Tea, please.}
\end{quote}

\subsection*{The letters in this word}
\textbf{\gu{ચ}} \emph{cha} — the same letter that opened \emph{chār}, \textquotedblleft{}four,\textquotedblright{} and sat inside \emph{vichār} — plus the long-\emph{ā} sign. Two letters, both already yours.

\begin{cousinweb}
\textbf{\gu{ચા}} is a loanword — unlike \textbf{pāṇī}, which Gujarati has owned since Sanskrit. It came through Classical Persian \emph{chā}, from Mandarin Chinese \textbf{chá}. That is the \textbf{overland} route, out through Central Asia and Persia: Hindi and Urdu \emph{chāy}, Russian \emph{chai}, Turkish \emph{çay} all took the same road and the same syllable.

There is another route entirely. Chinese merchants on the coast spoke a different dialect, Hokkien, where the same word is \emph{tê}. Dutch sailors picked that form up by \textbf{sea} and carried it into Europe: English \textbf{tea}, French \emph{thé}, German \emph{Tee}. One plant, one original Chinese word, and two pronunciations of it, sorted by whether a language met the word on a caravan route or a ship's deck. Gujarati's \emph{chā} and English \emph{tea} are, in that exact sense, the same word taken two different ways out of the same country.
\end{cousinweb}

\subsection*{Your turn}
\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item \emph{Say it:} \textbf{chā} — tea, and \textbf{chā, meherbānī karīne} — tea, please
  \item \emph{Run through:} both requests — \textbf{pāṇī, meherbānī karīne}; \textbf{chā, meherbānī karīne}
  \item \emph{Trace it:} Chinese \emph{chá} $\to$ Persian \emph{chā} $\to$ \textbf{\gu{ચા}}, the overland road
  \item \emph{Name:} one language that took the sea road instead, and its word (English, \textbf{tea})
\end{itemize}

\begin{tcolorbox}[breakable,colback=teal!4,colframe=teal!35!black,title={Before you move on}]
Ask for tea politely. (\emph{Chā, meherbānī karīne.}) Did \emph{chā} come by land or by sea? (\textbf{Land} — through Persian, from Mandarin.) Which English word for the same plant took the sea route instead, and through which language? (\textbf{Tea}, through Dutch.)

Sources: \href{https://en.wiktionary.org/wiki/\%E0\%AA\%9A\%E0\%AA\%BE}{Wiktionary: \gu{ચા}}; \href{https://www.etymonline.com/word/chai}{Etymonline: chai}.
\end{tcolorbox}
\section[dūdh]{\gu{દૂધ} — a verb frozen into a noun}

\label{lesson:GU-C10-dudh}



\begin{quote}
\textbf{\gu{પાણી}} was never borrowed. \textbf{\gu{ચા}} came the long way from China. The third drink is, like water, entirely Gujarati's own — but it got that way differently.
\end{quote}

\subsection*{You'll want to know first — one word}
\begin{quote}
\textbf{\gu{દૂધ}} — \emph{dūdh} — \textbf{milk}
\end{quote}

\begin{quote}
\textbf{\gu{દૂધ}, \gu{મહેરબાની} \gu{કરીને}.} — \emph{dūdh, meherbānī karīne.} — \textbf{Milk, please.}
\end{quote}

\subsection*{The letters in this word}
\textbf{\gu{દ}} \emph{da}, \textbf{\gu{ૂ}} the long-\emph{ū} sign below it, then \textbf{\gu{ધ}} \emph{dha} — the aspirated \emph{d}, the same puff of breath that made \textbf{\gu{ખ}} the aspirated \emph{k} and \textbf{\gu{ભ}} the aspirated \emph{b}. You have met the letter itself before, in \textbf{\gu{વાંધો} \gu{નહીં}}.

\begin{cousinweb}
\textbf{dūdh} comes from Sanskrit \textbf{dugdha}, and \emph{dugdha} is not, at root, a noun at all — it is the \textbf{past participle} of \textbf{duh-}, \textquotedblleft{}to milk,\textquotedblright{} so it means literally \textquotedblleft{}\textbf{milked}.\textquotedblright{} The action came first; the word for the substance is just that verb, frozen. It is the same trick \emph{gamvũ} played with \textquotedblleft{}to please,\textquotedblright{} run on a different part of speech: a verb collapsing into the thing it names.

The Indo-European root is *\emph{dheugh-}, \textquotedblleft{}to be fit, useful, of avail.\textquotedblright{} Its Germanic descendant did not go on to mean milk in English at all — it survives in \textbf{doughty}, \textquotedblleft{}valiant, capable,\textquotedblright{} from Old English \emph{dohtig}, \textquotedblleft{}of good use.\textquotedblright{} \emph{Dūdh} and \emph{doughty} are cousins by way of a root that once meant simply \textbf{being of use} — milk as \emph{the useful thing}, valor as \emph{the useful person}.
\end{cousinweb}

\subsection*{Your turn}
\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item \emph{Say it:} \textbf{dūdh} — milk, and \textbf{dūdh, meherbānī karīne} — milk, please
  \item \emph{Run through:} all three requests so far — \textbf{pāṇī}, \textbf{chā}, \textbf{dūdh}, each with \emph{meherbānī karīne}
  \item \emph{Trace it:} \emph{duh-} \textquotedblleft{}to milk\textquotedblright{} $\to$ \emph{dugdha} \textquotedblleft{}milked\textquotedblright{} $\to$ \textbf{dūdh}, and $\to$ English \textbf{doughty}
  \item \emph{Name:} which of the three drinks is a loanword (\textbf{\gu{ચા}}) and which two are not
\end{itemize}

\begin{tcolorbox}[breakable,colback=teal!4,colframe=teal!35!black,title={Before you move on}]
Ask for milk politely. (\emph{Dūdh, meherbānī karīne.}) What part of speech was \emph{dugdha} before it became a noun for milk? (A \textbf{past participle} — \textquotedblleft{}milked.\textquotedblright{}) Which unexpected English word for bravery shares its root with \emph{dūdh}? (\textbf{Doughty}.)

Sources: \href{https://en.wiktionary.org/wiki/\%E0\%AA\%A6\%E0\%AB\%82\%E0\%AA\%A7}{Wiktionary: \gu{દૂધ}}; \href{https://www.etymonline.com/word/doughty}{Etymonline: doughty}.
\end{tcolorbox}
\section[roṭlī]{\gu{રોટલી} — a request pattern, run four times}

\label{lesson:GU-C10-rotli}



\begin{quote}
Three drinks, one pattern: \textbf{pāṇī}, \textbf{chā}, \textbf{dūdh}, each followed by \emph{meherbānī karīne}. The fourth request is food, not drink, and it closes the chapter by finally breaking a pattern instead of continuing one.
\end{quote}

\subsection*{You'll want to know first — one word}
\begin{quote}
\textbf{\gu{રોટલી}} — \emph{roṭlī} — \textbf{flatbread}
\end{quote}

\begin{quote}
\textbf{\gu{રોટલી}, \gu{મહેરબાની} \gu{કરીને}.} — \emph{roṭlī, meherbānī karīne.} — \textbf{Bread, please.}
\end{quote}

\subsection*{The letters in this word}
\textbf{\gu{ર}} \emph{ra}, \textbf{\gu{ો}} the \emph{o} sign, then a new letter: \textbf{\gu{ટ}}, a retroflex \emph{ṭ} — the tongue curls back the way it does for \textbf{\gu{ણ}}, but here it stops the airflow instead of letting it through the nose. Then \textbf{\gu{લ}} \emph{la}, and \textbf{\gu{ી}} long-\emph{ī}. Headless throughout, like every letter you've met.

\begin{grammarlens}[title={Grammar Lens: an -ī that does not mean \textquotedblleft{}feminine, guaranteed\textquotedblright{}}]
\textbf{\gu{રોટલી}} is feminine, and its ending fits: many Gujarati nouns ending in \textbf{-ī} are feminine, the same \textbf{-ī} you saw mark the feminine adjective ending in \emph{sārī}. But you already own the counter-example: \textbf{\gu{પાણી}} also ends in \textbf{-ī}, and \emph{pāṇī} is \textbf{neuter}. The ending is a hint worth noticing, not a rule you can trust blind — every noun's gender has to be learned with the noun, the way \emph{madad karvī} forced \textbf{\gu{કરવી}} into its feminine shape only because \emph{madad} itself was feminine, not because of any ending on \emph{karvī} alone.
\end{grammarlens}

\begin{cousinweb}
\textbf{roṭlī} is inherited from Sanskrit \textbf{roṭikā}, \textquotedblleft{}a kind of bread.\textquotedblright{} That much is certain. What \emph{roṭikā} itself comes from is not: the standard comparative dictionaries weigh an unattested root meaning \textquotedblleft{}to strike against\textquotedblright{} against another meaning \textquotedblleft{}to crush,\textquotedblright{} and neither Turner nor Mayrhofer picks a winner.

That gives this chapter its own three-way dial, the same shape \emph{jāṇvũ}, \emph{levũ}, and \emph{khāvũ} once drew for verbs: \textbf{pāṇī} and \textbf{dūdh} are inherited straight from Sanskrit with a full etymology behind them; \textbf{chā} is a loan, traceable to Mandarin by a known road; \textbf{roṭlī} is inherited too, but its own root is where recorded history simply stops.
\end{cousinweb}

\subsection*{Your turn}
\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item \emph{Say it:} \textbf{roṭlī, meherbānī karīne} — bread, please
  \item \emph{Run through:} all four requests — \textbf{pāṇī}, \textbf{chā}, \textbf{dūdh}, \textbf{roṭlī}, each with \emph{meherbānī karīne}
  \item \emph{Sort:} inherited with a known root (\textbf{pāṇī}, \textbf{dūdh}), loaned (\textbf{chā}), inherited with an unknown root (\textbf{roṭlī})
  \item \emph{Contrast:} \textbf{roṭlī} feminine by its \textbf{-ī}, \textbf{pāṇī} neuter despite its \textbf{-ī}
\end{itemize}

\begin{tcolorbox}[breakable,colback=teal!4,colframe=teal!35!black,title={Before you move on}]
Ask for bread politely. (\emph{Roṭlī, meherbānī karīne.}) Does \emph{roṭikā}'s own root have a settled answer? (\textbf{No} — the dictionaries disagree and leave it open.) Name one Gujarati noun ending in \textbf{-ī} that is feminine and one that is neuter. (\textbf{Roṭlī}; \textbf{pāṇī}.) Run all four requests from this chapter. (\emph{Pāṇī}, \emph{chā}, \emph{dūdh}, \emph{roṭlī}, each with \emph{meherbānī karīne}.)

Sources: \href{https://en.wiktionary.org/wiki/\%E0\%AA\%B0\%E0\%AB\%8B\%E0\%AA\%9F\%E0\%AA\%B2\%E0\%AB\%80}{Wiktionary: \gu{રોટલી}}; \href{https://en.wiktionary.org/wiki/\%E0\%A4\%B0\%E0\%A5\%8B\%E0\%A4\%9F\%E0\%A4\%BF\%E0\%A4\%95\%E0\%A4\%BE}{Wiktionary: Sanskrit rotika}.
\end{tcolorbox}
